title: Acceptance Address on Behalf of the Schools
text:
ACCEPTANCE ADDRESS ON BEHALF OF THE SCHOOLS

By J. Wesley Moulton, Superintendent of Savoy Schools

Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:

As several speakers have already told you, today is a red-letter day in the history of Savoy, the greatest day, perhaps, in the history of this little town. A day that we have all been looking forward to with eagerness and anticipation for all these months.

Perhaps we Americans people are an impatient people, when everything does not happen just as we think it should, and I am afraid some of us had decided that this building would never be completed; that we had a "white elephant" on our hands, but I am happy to say that we were wrong and here is this magnificent building for your inspection and approval. We do not believe that there is a single man, woman, boy, or girl in Savoy or surrounding communities whose heart is not overflowing with gratitude and pride as they behold this magnificent building. Yes! We are proud of it, and why shouldn't we be? You have just heard Mr. Thomasson tell you that out of about 50 such buildings that have been constructed under his administration that this is one of the very best, if not the best. And you have also heard him present it to us without obligation, but we do feel a great sense of responsibility as a school, as a town, and as citizens, to use this building. Yes, but also to take care of it, and we promise you that as long as it lasts and we are in charge of it, it shall not be neglected, nor allowed to be torn up and run down, but kept in such condition that you will feel just as proud of it ten years from now as you do today.

We are connected with this school in a vital way, and naturally feel some concern about its administration, and so forth, and have given much time to study and meditation about it. We feel that this is a building which has been constructed in the discussion that has been going on these past months as to what kind of a school this is to be, and what attitude the school is to take toward religion, and so forth. And let me say in the beginning, this is not, never has been, and never will be, a Godless school, or a school where religion will be ignored or treated lightly. Far be it from such. We feel keenly our responsibility in the matter of religion, and as far as we are concerned, religion shall always be respected and reverenced here.

Perhaps, who knows, but in some future time that this school, through the aid of some good teacher, and this magnificent building, may develop another Robert Halsell, Sam McSpadden, or some such other character.
notes: Acceptance address by Savoy Schools Superintendent J. Wesley Moulton at the 1938 reunion dedication.
